name: Greenish Black
lede: Greenish Black is one of the named blacks in Werner's nomenclature of colors, the mineralogist's vocabulary of the 1770s, and its swatch on a screen is a neutral dark grey with no green in it at all.

sections.title: A black in Werner's list
sections.body:
Abraham Gottlob Werner devised his color nomenclature in 1774 to help identify minerals, starting from 54 terms and revising them for about forty years [1]. Patrick Syme later expanded the list to 108 terms in 1814 and 110 in 1821, adding a painted swatch and examples from the animal, vegetable and mineral worlds for each [1]. Greenish Black is number 19, in the section of whites, greys and blacks [2].

Syme's recipe starts from velvet black and adds small amounts of brown, yellow and green [2]. His examples are the breast of the lapwing, the mineral hornblende, and the bracts of the artichoke, drawn from Weinmann's *Phytanthoza iconographia* of 1737 [2]. Earlier tables by Lenz and Widenmann already list it, and one list in Baty's reproductions gives the alternative name raven-black [3]. Baty's index sends the reader to it on several pages, among them 8, 40, 62-3, 67 and 130 [2].

sections.title: Greenish black outside Werner
sections.body:
The phrase outlived the system, because dark minerals really do come in it. The Pigment Compendium describes hornblende as a dark green or greenish-black amphibole mineral, and brochantite, a copper mineral found in Cornwall and Derbyshire, as ranging from emerald green to greenish black [4]. Salter wrote in 1869 that bronze green, a species of Prussian green, looks greenish-black in deep washes, with a coppery cast [4].

Medicine borrowed the scale too. In 1827 the Nuremberg dermatologist Heinrich Eichhorn listed skin colors in disease using Werner's vocabulary, among them black, hornblende black or greenish black [5]. It is a reminder that these names were meant as tools for matching, not as poetry.

sections.title: Why the swatch is grey
sections.body:
The swatch here, #454445, is a scan of an aged Werner swatch, and our library notes it as approximate [6]. Its measured chroma is about 1, so on screen it reads as a neutral dark grey, and the nearest named color is [[charcoal]], 8.1 units away [6]. ISCC-NBS 1955 files it with its own black block [6].

Two effects explain the missing green. Old pigments and paper change over two centuries, and a faint tint is the first thing to vanish on a screen. Neighbors in Werner's row make the same point: [[bluish-black]] is the black with a little blue, and [[greyish-black]] the one softened with grey [2]. The three are hard to tell apart on a screen, and were meant to be told apart by eye against a black object.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,674 works, or 7.0 per cent [7]. It is mostly a shadow color, 63 per cent of the time, and a mid-tone in 35 per cent [7]. The largest cover is a portrait of 1821 by Ammi Phillips, at 83 per cent, followed by a Japanese painting of the descent of Amida Buddha, of 1270, at 77 per cent [7].

The lift grows in the twentieth century: 272 of 1,674 works from the 1900s, or 16.2 per cent, against 5.3 per cent of the 1400s, and the 1910s peak at 19.1 per cent [7]. Danish and Norwegian paintings carry it most, 247 of 1,676 and 25 of 120, and among individual painters Hammershøi has it in 19 of 50 works and Derain in 9 of 22 [7]. A neutral dark like this matches many blacks, and old varnish darkens pictures further, so it is a marker for dark pictures and not for any pigment [7].

In print, *greenish black* peaked around 1926 and has fallen to about 13 per cent of that peak by 2000 [8].

questions.q: According to Baty, Syme's recipe for Greenish Black starts from velvet black.

openers: Greenish black was a mineralogist's name: Werner's examples include the mineral hornblende and a lapwing's breast.
Where to look: dark portraits and shadows often hold a black that is a little tinted, not neutral.

issues: Only Baty and the Pigment Compendium discuss it; article short by design.
The sentence about aging pigments and screens is interpretation, uncited.
